set_title: Breathing patterns: Kussmaul, Cheyne-Stokes, Biot, apneustic and central neurogenic
stem: A 71-year-old man with heart failure (ejection fraction 20%) is watched overnight. His breathing slowly deepens, then grows shallower, then stops for 20 seconds before the cycle repeats. The nurse charts Cheyne-Stokes breathing.
oneliner: 71M, heart failure with EF 20% + Cheyne-Stokes breathing at night → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains this breathing pattern?

options.B: Loss of pontine signals that end inspiration
options.C: Damage to the medullary respiratory rhythm generator
options.D: Upper airway collapse during sleep despite effort
options.E: Delayed CO2 feedback from slow circulation

whyNot.A: That is Kussmaul breathing; his pattern **deepens, fades and pauses**
whyNot.B: That causes apneustic breathing; his breaths **slowly deepen and fade**, never held
whyNot.C: That causes chaotic Biot breathing; his cycle **repeats regularly**
whyNot.D: Obstructive apnea shows effort against a closed airway; his breathing **simply stops**

answer: Delayed CO2 feedback from slow circulation
why: Breaths crescendo, decrescendo, then pause. Slow blood flow in heart failure delays CO2 signals to the chemoreceptors, so breathing overshoots and then undershoots.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Breaths swell, fade, then pause; repeats
Irregular breaths and pauses, no pattern
Lower pons lesion, e.g. basilar stroke
Fast deep breaths without metabolic acidosis

idea.rule: Waxing-waning breaths with apneas in heart failure = Cheyne-Stokes from delayed feedback.
also: Also after bilateral cerebral hemisphere damage
Common during sleep at high altitude

set_title: Pulse signs: paradoxus, alternans, parvus et tardus, water-hammer and bisferiens
stem: A 48-year-old woman with metastatic lung cancer has 2 days of worsening breathlessness. Pulse is 124/min and blood pressure 92/60 mm Hg. Neck veins are distended and heart sounds are muffled. Systolic pressure is 92 mm Hg on expiration and 76 mm Hg on inspiration.
oneliner: 48F, lung cancer + JVD, muffled heart sounds, systolic 92 → 76 on inspiration → ?

whyNot.A: Alternans varies beat to beat; her pressure falls **with each inspiration**
whyNot.B: Parvus et tardus is a weak, late upstroke; her pressure falls **only on inspiration**
whyNot.C: Water-hammer pulse bounds with a wide pulse pressure; hers is **92/60**
whyNot.E: Bisferiens has two peaks per beat; her systolic pressure **drops 16 mm Hg on inspiration**

why: A 16 mm Hg inspiratory systolic fall is pulsus paradoxus. Fluid fixes total heart volume, so inspiratory right heart filling bows the septum and cuts left ventricular output.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Inspiratory systolic BP drop over 10 mm Hg
Regular rhythm, strong and weak beats alternate
Weak carotid pulse that peaks late
Bounding pulse that rises and collapses fast
Two systolic peaks in each beat

idea.rule: Inspiratory systolic drop over 10 mm Hg + JVD + muffled sounds = tamponade.
also: Beck triad: hypotension, JVD, muffled sounds

set_title: Pulse signs: paradoxus, alternans, parvus et tardus, water-hammer and bisferiens
stem: A 76-year-old man has had dizziness and chest tightness while climbing stairs for 3 months. His carotid pulse is weak and rises slowly to a late peak (pulsus parvus et tardus). S2 is soft and single.
oneliner: 76M, exertional dizziness and chest tightness + pulsus parvus et tardus, soft single S2 → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: Regurgitation gives a bounding, collapsing pulse, not a **weak, slow-rising** one
whyNot.C: Tamponade causes pulsus paradoxus; his finding is a **slow, late carotid peak**
whyNot.D: HCM gives a brisk, two-peaked pulse; his pulse is **weak and rises slowly**
whyNot.E: Dilated cardiomyopathy gives pulsus alternans; his clue is a **late peak with soft single S2**

why: A narrowed aortic valve slows left ventricular ejection, so the carotid pulse is small and late. Exertional angina, syncope and dyspnea follow the fixed outflow.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Inspiratory systolic BP drop over 10 mm Hg
Regular rhythm, strong and weak beats alternate
Weak carotid pulse that peaks late
Bounding pulse that rises and collapses fast
Two systolic peaks in each beat

idea.rule: Weak, late carotid pulse + soft single S2 in an older adult = aortic stenosis.
also: Crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids

set_title: Pulse signs: paradoxus, alternans, parvus et tardus, water-hammer and bisferiens
stem: A 34-year-old man with Marfan syndrome has tired easily for a year. Blood pressure is 164/42 mm Hg. When the examiner raises his arm and grips the forearm, the pulse strikes the fingers hard and then falls away abruptly. His head bobs with each heartbeat.
oneliner: 34M, Marfan + BP 164/42, hard pulse that falls away abruptly, head bobbing → ?

whyNot.A: Paradoxus is an inspiratory BP fall; his clue is **164/42 with a collapsing pulse**
whyNot.B: Alternans swaps strong and weak beats; **every beat strikes hard**
whyNot.C: Parvus et tardus is weak and slow; his pulse **strikes the fingers hard**
whyNot.D: Bisferiens is felt as two peaks; his pulse **falls away abruptly** after one

why: A hard, fast-rising pulse that collapses is the water-hammer (Corrigan) pulse. A large stroke volume raises systolic pressure; backflow into the ventricle drops diastolic pressure fast.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Inspiratory systolic BP drop over 10 mm Hg
Regular rhythm, strong and weak beats alternate
Weak carotid pulse that peaks late
Bounding pulse that rises and collapses fast
Two systolic peaks in each beat

idea.rule: Wide pulse pressure + bounding, collapsing pulse = chronic aortic regurgitation.

set_title: Pulse signs: paradoxus, alternans, parvus et tardus, water-hammer and bisferiens
stem: A 66-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy has worsening dyspnea. Ejection fraction is 15%. ECG shows regular sinus rhythm. The radial pulse shows pulsus alternans: strong and weak beats alternate.
oneliner: 66M, dilated cardiomyopathy, EF 15%, sinus rhythm + pulsus alternans → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains this sign?

options.B: Fluid restricting filling of all chambers
options.C: Fixed obstruction at the aortic valve
options.D: Large diastolic backflow across the aortic valve
options.E: Dynamic septal obstruction of LV outflow

whyNot.B: That is tamponade, giving pulsus paradoxus; he has **dilated cardiomyopathy, EF 15%**
whyNot.C: Aortic stenosis gives a slow, weak pulse; his beats **alternate strong and weak**
whyNot.D: Regurgitation bounds on every beat; his **strong and weak beats alternate**
whyNot.E: HCM obstruction gives a two-peaked pulse; his ventricle is **dilated with EF 15%**

why: In regular rhythm, alternating strong and weak beats mean a failing left ventricle whose contractile force swings from beat to beat.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Inspiratory systolic BP drop over 10 mm Hg
Regular rhythm, strong and weak beats alternate
Weak carotid pulse that peaks late
Bounding pulse that rises and collapses fast
Two systolic peaks in each beat

idea.rule: Alternating pulse strength in sinus rhythm = severe LV systolic dysfunction.
also: Poor prognostic sign in heart failure
